o1.biggest_strength: The decision and the numbers come first: 3.2% vs 0.25% conversion, the 13% fall in organic clicks, and what the lost blog clicks were worth. The week 1 plan is Monday-ready with a draft title, meta, and outline in our voice, and the plan includes rollback and measurement rules.
o1.biggest_mistake: It tells the writer to leave decaying posts alone. It never says to merge or redirect them. It also makes no case for a GA4 data-migration page, which is Maya's biggest worry. It is also a little long for the 1,000-word cap.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Add a stop-or-redirect rule for the decaying blog posts. Add a 'moving from GA4 without losing history' page for Maya. Trim to under 1,000 words. Keep the conservative trial forecast by month and the dated draft title and meta.

o2.biggest_strength: Clean trials-per-1,000-clicks table and a well-ranked list with paid-customer figures. It adds a GA4 history page for Maya's main fear and a rule to merge or redirect dead posts, and every month is mapped to the 12-page limit.
o2.biggest_mistake: The forecasts are optimistic. Moving /vs-google-analytics to a 9% CTR gives +100 trials, and the plan then calls the sum of these a 'ceiling'. Month 3 is vague ('pick two competitors'). The week 1 plan has no concrete title or meta draft. It also sends the draft to me for a facts check when I'm unavailable.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Use realistic forecasts per month. Write the actual title and meta in week 1. Name the Month 3 pages. Cut the developer-day tasks to what one day can really hold. Keep the GA4 history page and the redirect rule.

reason: Output 1 is more realistic and more ready to hand to the writer on Monday, with a draft title and meta, a ranked table, and clear rollback rules. Output 2 has better ideas on Maya's data worry and on redirecting dead posts, but its forecasts are rosier and its first week is less concrete.
